temptingClaims: A grain's distance from its starting point follows the same bell curve as its displacement along one axis.
whyTempting: § 4 finds that the displacements follow the law of random errors, and the bell curve is the familiar picture of that law.
whereItIsTrue: Along any one axis. The paper's law is for the displacement in the direction of the X-axis, and that distribution is the one of random errors, centred at zero.

whatIsTrue.r0: The bell curve is the law along one axis. The distance from the start, in space, is not a bell curve centred at zero: a grain is least likely of all to be found right back at its starting point.
whatIsTrue.r1: § 4's distribution is for the change of one coordinate, and it is the same as that of random errors, as was to be expected (pp. 558–559). The distance from the starting point combines three such coordinates. Its root mean square is \(\lambda_x\sqrt{3}\), as the paper remarks for the total displacements (p. 559). The density of distances in space is zero at the starting point and largest at a positive distance, because a thin shell of radius \(r\) holds a volume in proportion to \(r^2\). BM-06 computes the radial statistics: after one second at its modern preset, \(\lambda_x\) is 0.927 μm and the root-mean-square distance in space 1.605 μm, the factor \(\sqrt{3}\) of the paper.
whatIsTrue.r2: (1) Along the X-axis the displacement has the Gaussian density \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi Dt}}e^{-x^2/4Dt}\), largest at \(x = 0\). (2) In space the three coordinates are independent, each with that law, so the density at a point \((x, y, z)\) is their product, largest at the start. (3) The distance \(r\) gathers every point of a sphere of radius \(r\), whose area is \(4\pi r^2\). The density of distances is therefore \(4\pi r^2\,(4\pi Dt)^{-3/2}\,e^{-r^2/4Dt}\), which is zero at \(r = 0\). (4) Its mean square is the sum over the three axes, \(3 \cdot 2Dt = 6Dt\), so its root mean square is \(\sqrt{3}\,\lambda_x\), the paper's \(\lambda_x\sqrt{3}\). (5) A bell curve in \(r\) would put the most likely distance at zero; the law in space puts it at \(2\sqrt{Dt}\).
whatIsTrue.r3: The paper states only the one-axis law and the factor \(\sqrt{3}\) for the total. The density of distances is a step anyone can take from its premises; BM-06 draws it beside the one-axis curve.

sources: A. Einstein, Ann. Phys. (4) 17, 549–560 (1905), plates pp. 558–559

BM-06 preset bm-06-modern-one-second: λx 9.268e-7 m, root-mean-square radius in three dimensions 1.605e-6 m = √3 λx; radialPropagator3d at r = 0 is 0 (moments and radialPropagator3d, modern-si-2019 constants)
